name: The Queen's Gambit
blurb: Offer a pawn you are not really giving away, to trade a wing pawn for the centre.

steps.note: 1.d4. Compared to 1.e4 this is the slower start: the pawn is defended by the queen from move one, so the centre is harder to knock over and the games last longer before anything is decided.

1...d5 is the symmetrical, principled reply. Both sides have a protected pawn in the centre, and neither can easily be dislodged — so White has to find a way to challenge d5 that does not just trade everything off.

2.c4 is the Queen's Gambit, and the name is a bit of a lie: it is not a real gambit. If Black takes with 2...dxc4, White does not have to sacrifice anything — the pawn can be won back at leisure, as the next few moves show. What White is really offering is a trade of a *wing* pawn for a *centre* pawn, which is a good deal even when nothing is sacrificed at all.

2...e6 declines: the Queen's Gambit Declined, one of the most respected defences in chess. Black shores up d5 with a pawn and accepts the same cost the French pays — the light-squared bishop is now behind its own pawns and will need work to free.
3.Nc3 adds a third attacker to d5 and develops toward the centre. White is not in a hurry; every move here does one straightforward job.
3...Nf6 defends d5 a second time and develops. Both sides are simply piling pieces onto the one square the whole opening is about.

4.Bg5 is the classical move, and it is an attack on d5 by indirect means: the bishop pins the knight on f6 against the queen, so the knight has stopped defending d5. Learning to see that a pinned piece is not really defending anything is worth more than memorising this line.

4...Be7 breaks the pin the simple way, by putting a piece in between and preparing to castle. Black is solid, slightly passive, and entirely fine — which is the Queen's Gambit Declined in one sentence.

5.e3 is modest and correct: it opens the f1 bishop and reinforces d4. White has a small, durable space advantage and a plan of Nf3, Bd3 and castling. Nothing dramatic — the Queen's Gambit wins games by being slightly better for forty moves.

Back to move two, and the other main answer. 2...dxc4 is the Queen's Gambit Accepted. Black takes the pawn, and the honest reason is not greed — it is that giving up the centre buys time to develop quickly and hit d4.

3.Nf3 first, and this move order matters. The immediate 3.e3 invites 3...b5, when Black tries to hang on to the extra pawn; the knight move controls e5 and prepares to take the pawn back without that argument.
3...Nf6 develops and stops White playing e4 with everything at once. Black is not trying to keep the pawn — holding it with ...b5 and ...c6 costs so much time that the position falls apart.
4.e3 opens the bishop's path to c4, where it will recapture. White has spent no material and no time, and now has two centre pawns against one.

4...e6 5.Bxc4, and the pawn is back. Count what the gambit actually achieved: White has pawns on d4 and e3 against Black's on e6, a bishop developed to an active square with tempo, and no material deficit at any point. That is why 2.c4 is not really a gambit, and why it has been the main way to play 1.d4 for a hundred and fifty years.
